title: Reproducibility
story:
Reproducibility means being able to produce the same result again from a recorded state. In a system whose central component samples from a distribution, that requires deliberate work, and the work is worth doing for a plain reason: without it, you cannot investigate anything. A bad answer that cannot be reproduced is a bad answer that cannot be diagnosed, only discussed.

Begin with the part that is entirely in your hands, which is more of it than people assume. Everything except the sampling is deterministic if you record it: the exact input as assembled, the prompt version, which documents retrieval returned and from which index built at which time, the tool results, the decoding settings, the model version. When all of that is stored with the request, most investigations become straightforward, because you can rebuild the situation exactly and look at it rather than reasoning about what probably happened.

Then the sampling. Randomness in generation is controllable in principle — a fixed seed with the same input and the same settings should give the same output — and it is only as good as the promise underneath it, which varies. Hosted services may not expose a seed, may change the serving stack, and may batch your request differently on two occasions in a way that alters the result. Assume you may not get bit-for-bit repetition, and design for the weaker property you can actually have: the same recorded inputs, replayed, producing an answer you can compare, and a stored copy of the original answer for when they differ.

That stored copy is the practical heart of this lesson. Keep what the system actually produced, alongside everything that produced it. It costs storage and it is the difference between an investigation and a conversation, because a comparison needs both terms and the past is not otherwise available.

Distinguish two things people conflate, because they need different treatment. Reproducing a single request is a debugging capability and needs per-request records. Reproducing an evaluation is a comparison capability and needs the case set, the scores, the outputs and the full configuration stored together as one artefact. A score without the configuration that produced it is not a measurement you can return to; it is a number that was true once, under conditions nobody wrote down.

Pin the things that are not the model too, because they move as readily. The index and when it was built, the chunking strategy, the embedding model and its version, the retrieval parameters, the versions of the libraries in the path. A result reproduced against a different index is not reproduced, and this is the most common way an investigation quietly goes wrong — the code was pinned, the data was not, and nobody thought of the corpus as a version at all.

And be honest in what you claim. If your system cannot give bit-for-bit repetition, say that, rather than implying determinism you do not have. What you can usually promise is that given the same recorded state you will get a result of the same character, and that any difference is visible because the original was stored. That is a weaker guarantee than determinism and it is enough to run a serious system on, provided everybody knows which one they have.

problem.name: Recreating a result from a recorded state
problem.shape: Something happened once and has to be examined afterwards, in a system that samples.
tell: a reported bad answer cannot be reproduced and so cannot be diagnosed
an evaluation score exists without the configuration that produced it
the code was pinned for an investigation and the index was not
determinism is being claimed for a path that includes a hosted service
problem.move: Record everything except the sampling — assembled input, prompt version, retrieved documents, index identity and build time, tool results, decoding settings, model version — store the output that was actually produced, and keep evaluation results as one artefact containing the configuration, the cases, the scores and the outputs.
problem.invariant: Everything but the sampling is deterministic given the recorded state, so the fraction of an investigation that depends on luck is the fraction you failed to record.
problem.breaks: A hosted service may not expose a seed, may change its serving stack, and may batch requests differently, so bit-for-bit repetition is not a property you can assume.

cost.time: capturing state on every request, and storing artefacts for evaluations rather than scores alone
cost.space: full inputs, outputs and retrieved documents per request, which is the real cost and the thing that makes investigation possible
cost.beats: logging the final answer only, which shows the symptom and nothing that caused it

problem.practice: Take a request from last week and try to replay it exactly: same assembled input, same retrieved documents, same settings, same versions. Note every piece you had to guess at. Each guess is a field you are not recording, and the list is usually short enough to fix in a morning.

beats.broke: The component that generates samples, so a result cannot be recreated and a bad answer can only be discussed rather than diagnosed.
beats.fix: Record everything but the sampling with each request, store the output that was produced, and keep evaluations as one artefact containing configuration, cases, scores and outputs.
beats.cost: Storage for full inputs, outputs and retrieved documents, and the discipline of pinning the index and the corpus as versions alongside the code.

interview.trap: Pinning the code and forgetting the corpus. A result reproduced against a differently built index is not reproduced, and this is the usual way an investigation silently goes wrong.
